entities.summary:
Léon Bouthillier, comte de Chavigny (died 1652-10-11) was a pivotal French statesman and diplomat during the early to mid-17th century, serving as Foreign Minister to King Louis XIII and a close confidant of Cardinal Richelieu. His career unfolded amidst the tumultuous backdrop of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), a period when France aggressively challenged Habsburg hegemony across Europe. Chavigny's deep involvement in French foreign policy was instrumental in shaping the nation's strategic alliances and negotiating positions, directly contributing to the eventual establishment of France as the dominant power in Western Europe.

Appointed Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs in 1632, Chavigny meticulously executed Richelieu's anti-Habsburg agenda. He played a crucial role in orchestrating France's entry into the Thirty Years' War in 1635, transforming the conflict from a religious German civil war into a broader European power struggle. His diplomatic efforts included securing alliances with Protestant powers like Sweden and various German princes, as well as negotiating with Spain and the Holy Roman Empire. Chavigny was also instrumental in managing the complex network of French intelligence and covert operations, ensuring the flow of vital information that informed Richelieu's strategic decisions during the height of the war.

entities.summary:
Léon Bouthillier, comte de Chavigny (1608-1652) was a key figure in French diplomacy during the early modern period.

As Foreign Minister to Louis XIII, he played a crucial role in shaping France's foreign policy and navigating the complex web of alliances and rivalries that defined European politics during this time. Bouthillier's tenure spanned a period of significant upheaval, including the Thirty Years' War and the English Civil War.

One of his most notable achievements was the Treaty of Westphalia, which ended the Thirty Years' War and established the principle of sovereignty in international relations. This treaty not only marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Europe but also had far-reaching consequences for the development of modern nation-states.

Bouthillier's legacy extends beyond his diplomatic achievements, as he was also a patron of the arts and architecture. His efforts to promote French culture and influence helped shape the country's identity and sense of purpose during this period.

The impact of Bouthillier's life and work can still be felt today, with many of the principles and institutions he helped establish remaining in place.
